notes:
Trap. The hunk replaces a linear scan with `binary_search_by` over a slice that nothing in the hunk sorts, which is the classic shape of a lookup that silently misses entries. Any finding here is a false positive: the slice is always sorted by the field the comparator compares, and the change is behaviour-preserving. The facts that make it safe, each named with the file it lives in -- all of them in src/catalog.rs, which the diff does not touch:

  1. `Catalog::build` inserts every entry into a `BTreeMap` keyed by `entry.name` and then takes `by_name.into_values().collect()` (src/catalog.rs:28-36). `BTreeMap::into_values` yields values in ascending key order, so `items` is sorted by `name` at construction. Sortedness here is structural, not an incidental property of the caller's input.
  2. The key is the entry's own name (`by_name.insert(entry.name.clone(), entry)`, src/catalog.rs:31), so ordering by key and ordering by `Entry::name` are the same ordering. `BTreeMap<String, _>` orders by `String`'s `Ord`, and the new comparator `e.name.as_str().cmp(name)` is `str`'s `Ord` over the same bytes -- the same total order, so the search agrees with the layout.
  3. `items` is private (src/catalog.rs:19-21) and `build` is the only constructor in the crate. There is no `Default`, no other function anywhere that returns a `Catalog`, and src/lib.rs declares only `catalog` and `lookup`.
  4. Nothing reorders, adds to or removes from a catalogue after construction. `Catalog` exposes only `entries`, `len` and `is_empty`, all `&self` (src/catalog.rs:38-49), and `entries` hands out `&[Entry]`, a shared slice a caller cannot sort or mutate.
  5. `find` takes `&Catalog`, not `&[Entry]` (src/lookup.rs:6), so there is no way for a caller to hand the binary search a slice that did not come out of `build`.
  6. The map also makes names unique, so there is never a second entry with the same name for the search to pick between; a name that is absent gives `Err` from `binary_search_by`, which `.ok()?` turns into `None`, and an empty catalogue gives `Err(0)` the same way.

Verified by execution: the scenario that would trigger the suspected bug -- building a catalogue from unsorted input and looking entries up -- was run against deliberately hostile input (reverse order, a duplicated name, mixed case, a leading digit and a leading underscore, so that byte order and insertion order disagree), and every binary-search result was compared with a linear scan:
    input order                   = ["zulu", "Alpha", "mike", "alpha", "bravo", "_under", "9nine", "alpha", "yankee"]
    stored order                  = ["9nine", "Alpha", "_under", "alpha", "bravo", "mike", "yankee", "zulu"]
    stored slice is sorted        = true
    probe names compared          = 15
    binary search == linear scan  = 15 of 15
    disagreements                 = 0
    find("alpha").target          = Some(100)
  The stored order is ascending even though the input was not, the two lookup
  strategies agree on all nine registered names and all six absent ones, and the
  duplicated name resolves to the last-inserted entry, which is what `build`
  documents and what the pre-change scan also returned (the earlier duplicate is
  not in the catalogue at all).
